{{short description|American mathematician}}
'''William A. Veech''' was the Edgar O. Lovett Professor of Mathematics at [[Rice University]]<ref name="profile">[http://report.rice.edu/sir/faculty.detail?p=A6B7D13019ABFD4C Faculty profile], Rice University, retrieved 2015-03-01.</ref> until his death.  His research concerned [[dynamical system]]s; he is particularly known for his work on [[interval exchange transformation]]s, and is the namesake of the [[Veech surface]]. He died unexpectedly on August 30, 2016 in Houston, Texas.<ref name="death">{{cite web | url=http://www.ricethresher.org/article/2016/09/former-math-department-chair-passes-away | title=Former math department chair passes away | publisher=Rice Thresher | access-date=29 September 2016 | author=Todd, Hannah | date=21 September 2016 }}</ref>

==Education==
Veech graduated from [[Dartmouth College]] in 1960,<ref name="profile"/> and earned his Ph.D. in 1963 from [[Princeton University]] under the supervision of [[Salomon Bochner]].<ref name="profile"/><ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=8126}}</ref>

==Contributions==
An [[interval exchange transformation]] is a [[dynamical system]] defined from a partition of the [[unit interval]] into finitely many smaller intervals, and a [[permutation]] on those intervals. Veech and [[Howard Masur]] independently discovered that, for almost every partition and every irreducible permutation, these systems are [[Ergodic theory|uniquely ergodic]], and also made contributions to the theory of weak mixing for these systems.<ref>{{citation|contribution=Prevalence|first1=B. R.|last1=Hunt|first2=V. Yu.|last2=Kaloshin|title=Handbook of Dynamical Systems, Volume 3|editor1-first=H.|editor1-last=Broer|editor1-link=Henk Broer|editor2-first=F.|editor2-last=Takens|editor3-first=B.|editor3-last=Hasselblatt|publisher=Elsevier|year=2010|isbn=9780080932262|pages=43–88}}. See in particular [https://books.google.com/books?id=mJYw3u2HniUC&pg=PA51 p.&nbsp;51].</ref> The Rauzy–Veech–Zorich induction map, a function from and to the space of interval exchange transformations is named in part after Veech: Rauzy defined the map, Veech constructed an infinite [[invariant measure]] for it, and Zorich strengthened Veech's result by making the measure finite.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Bufetov | first = Alexander I.
 | doi = 10.1090/S0894-0347-06-00528-5
 | issue = 3
 | journal = Journal of the American Mathematical Society
 | mr = 2220100
 | pages = 579–623
 | title = Decay of correlations for the Rauzy-Veech-Zorich induction map on the space of interval exchange transformations and the central limit theorem for the Teichmüller flow on the moduli space of abelian differentials
 | volume = 19
 | year = 2006| arxiv = math/0506222
 | s2cid = 15755696
 }}.</ref>

The [[Veech surface]] and the related Veech group are named after Veech, as is the Veech dichotomy according to which [[geodesic flow]] on the Veech surface is either periodic or ergodic.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Smillie | first1 = John
 | last2 = Weiss | first2 = Barak
 | doi = 10.1017/S0143385708000114
 | issue = 6
 | journal = Ergodic Theory and Dynamical Systems
 | mr = 2465608
 | pages = 1959–1972
 | title = Veech's dichotomy and the lattice property
 | volume = 28
 | year = 2008| s2cid = 42112090
 }}.</ref>

Veech played a role in the Nobel-prize-winning discovery of [[buckminsterfullerene]] in 1985 by a team of Rice University chemists including [[Richard Smalley]]. At that time, Veech was chair of the Rice mathematics department, and was asked by Smalley to identify the shape that the chemists had determined for this molecule. Veech answered, "I could explain this to you in a number of ways, but what you've got there, boys, is a soccer ball."<ref>{{citation|first=Edward|last=Edelson|title=Buckyball: the magic molecule|journal=[[Popular Science]]|date=August 1991|pages=52–57, 87}}. The quote is on [https://books.google.com/books?id=l3CxgWPR4j8C&pg=PA55 p.&nbsp;55].</ref><ref>{{citation|title=Designing the Molecular World: Chemistry at the Frontier|series=Princeton Science Library|first=Philip|last=Ball|authorlink=Philip Ball|publisher=Princeton University Press|year=1996|isbn=9780691029009|page=46|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tvP7hyVa2BwC&pg=PA46}}.</ref>

Veech is the author of ''A Second Course in Complex Analysis'' (W. A. Benjamin, 1967; Dover, 2008, {{ISBN|9780486462943}}).<ref>Review of ''A Second Course in Complex Analysis'' by E. Hille, {{MR|0220903}}.</ref><ref>{{citation|title=W. A. Veech, ''A Second Course in Complex Analysis''|department=Book Reviews|first=H.|last=Wenzel|journal=[[Journal of Applied Mathematics and Mechanics]]|date=1968 |volume=48|issue=7|pages=502–503|doi=10.1002/zamm.19680480725|bibcode=1968ZaMM...48..502W}}.</ref><ref>{{citation|title=''A Second Course in Complex Analysis'', William A. Veech|work=MAA Reviews|publisher=[[Mathematical Association of America]]|first=Allen|last=Stenger|date=April 24, 2008|url=http://www.maa.org/publications/maa-reviews/a-second-course-in-complex-analysis}}.</ref>

==Awards and honors==
In 2012, Veech became one of the inaugural [[fellow]]s of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[http://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180825194636/http://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list |date=2018-08-25 }}, retrieved 2015-03-01.</ref>
